title: True/False is a type, like number and text
idea: Booleans are a data type, alongside numbers and strings. The idea of types from earlier units applies here too.

exercises.prompt: We've met numbers and text. What type are True and False?
exercises.explanation: True and False form their own type: booleans. It sits alongside numbers and text.

exercises.prompt: Match each value to its type.
exercises.explanation: Every value has a type. 7 is a number, "hi" is text, True is a boolean.

exercises.prompt: A boolean is a different type from a number.
exercises.explanation: Yes. Booleans (True/False) are their own type, separate from numbers like 7.

exercises.prompt: Which list has ALL three value types we've seen?
exercises.explanation: 5 is a number, "cat" is text, True is a boolean - three different types together.

exercises.prompt:
What is the type of the value in this variable?

flag = False
exercises.explanation: flag holds False, which is a boolean value. The variable's current type is boolean.

exercises.prompt:
What is the type of the value in this variable?

count = 10
exercises.explanation: count holds 10, a number. A quick review that different values have different types.

exercises.prompt: "True" (in quotes) and True (no quotes) have the same type.
exercises.explanation: No - "True" is text (a string) and True is a boolean. Quotes change the type.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is a boolean value?
exercises.explanation: False (no quotes) is the boolean. "False" and "no" are text; 3.5 is a number.
Only True and False (no quotes) are booleans. "True" is text and 0 is a number.

exercises.prompt: Why does knowing the type of a value matter?
options: Because the computer treats each type differently
Because all types are the same
So we can ignore the value
exercises.explanation: Type decides what the computer can do with a value. A yes/no fact behaves differently from a number or text.
